newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila oil deregulation seen attracting investors.
newsitem.headline: Manila oil deregulation seen attracting investors.

text.p: Philippine President Fidel Ramos on Wednesday approved full deregulation of the oil industry, a move that analysts said would draw new players into the market and provide stiffer competition for existing ones.

But the decision, taken a month ahead of schedule, would not immediately threaten the position of industry leader Petron Corp or Pilipinas Shell Petroleum Corp and Caltex (Philippines) Inc, they said.

"Definitely, it will mean more players but it will take time for them to make their presence felt considering that the three existing players have long been in the market," said Spencer Yap, analyst at BPI Capital Corp.

Petron is 40 percent owned by Saudi Arabia's Aramco, while Pilipinas Shell is a unit of the Royal Dutch/Shell group and Caltex (Philippines), a unit of the joint venture between Texaco Inc and Chevron Corp.

Newer operators entering the market may seek to build a market outside Metro Manila due to the high cost of land in the capital and surrounding cities, Raul Ruiz, vice-president for research at Sun Hung Kai Securities, said.

Ramos' order on Wednesday setting February 8 as the date for full deregulation of the industry completes a process started last August when the government began dismantling controls that have been in place for two decades.
Under the controlled regime, prices were fixed by the government, allowing oil firms a maximum return of eight percent.
The cap on returns, as well as restrictions on imports and marketing of oil products, discouraged investors and kept the country's refining capacity at low levels.
Full deregulation was set for March this year but the government hastened it because a buffer fund meant to absorb the difference between international and local prices was exhausted.
Analysts said the long time needed to build oil facilities would allow existing companies to protect their market share for now.
According to industry data, Petron Corp has 41.3 percent of the market, Pilipinas Shell 33.7 percent and Caltex (Philippines) 24.8 percent.
Sun Hung Kai's Ruiz said an immediate benefit for these companies would be that the government would be forced to settle their claims on the buffer fund as soon as possible.
Under the regulated regime, oil companies were meant to claim the difference between international and local prices from the oil buffer fund, but the money ran out.
The fund now owes the three firms a total of 2.4 billion pesos ($92 million).

The government had kept these claims aside and poured a separate sum of one billion pesos ($38 million) into the fund which was meant to last during the partial de-control phase. That money was also exhausted, forcing the government to advance the full deregulation date.
